chapter: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
title: Peeping into the morning cabaret on State Street
summary: The boys lay on their stomachs to look down into a dive where people still danced at eight in the morning; Milt did the same on his paper route.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Now, there was another little cabaret we used to go and peep around 7 or 7:30, maybe around 8 o'clock in the morning, on State Street. We'd go there and we would lay on our stomach by the side... You'd go in there and you could look down and see these people in there dancing, still having a good time at 8 o'clock in the morning. I forget the name of it, but...
Was that the Entertainments? It might have been the Entertainments.

No, it was not that far. We hadn't got down to 47th Street in those days. It had to be 35th Street, 35th or 37th Street. 37th Street. Because we didn't get down to 47th Street until the Regal days. That's 1927.
Well, in 1921 my aunt lived at 48th Street.
But over on South Parkway, which was Grand Boulevard...
Yeah. Well, we weren't out that way. The cabarets weren't on State Street until... I believe. I don't remember any cabarets out that far. But it could be.
It wasn't a great big cabaret. It was like a little dive! A little club, like those places where Ollie Potter(?) played. What did they call that little place?

Yeah, one of them little funky joints. And you'd see them people in there with the women. We'd be up there looking down, layin' on our stomachs. And you had the window, see, right down here near the ground, just enough. And if you'd look down there... And we'd stare down. I guess people must have looked up and seen these two faces up there. I mean, we were on to everything, man.

I used to do that coming back from my newspaper route, and I would see the guys packing up their instruments, and I'd be looking in the windows, and the musicians would be standing around -- and it would be five or six o'clock in the morning, and I'd be out with my newspapers. I did the same thing.
